gemma4_verdict: Gemma 4 31B has a built-in 'Thinking' reasoning mode that emits a chain-of-thought (commonly 4,000+ tokens on hard problems) before the final answer. Per-request control depends heavily on the serving stack and is the messiest part of the comparison. In vLLM, Gemma 4 reasoning is DISABLED by default; you serve with --reasoning-parser gemma4 and enable it per-request via chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": true} (or via reasoning_effort low/medium/high, which vLLM auto-maps to enable_thinking=true; reasoning_effort="none" -> false). vLLM does NOT expose a clean per-request thinking-token budget for Gemma 4 — there is no first-class reasoning_budget request field that caps thinking tokens; budgeting is effectively via max_tokens plus enable_thinking on/off. In llama.cpp, the per-request token cap is the request-body field thinking_budget_tokens, which is only honored when the server was started WITHOUT --reasoning-budget (the source checks `if (reasoning_budget == -1 && body.contains("thinking_budget_tokens"))`). Per established Labmate context: for Gemma 4 in llama-server, enable_thinking:false via chat_template_kwargs is SILENTLY IGNORED — you must use the global --reasoning off flag to fully disable thinking; and thinking_budget_tokens is the correct per-request budget parameter (NOT reasoning_budget). Known llama.cpp bugs: Gemma 4 long-context can flood <unused49>/<|unused|> tokens, and disable-thinking flags sometimes still leak reasoning. So Gemma 4's per-request thinking control works but the reliable levers differ per backend: llama.cpp = thinking_budget_tokens (numeric cap) + global --reasoning off; vLLM = enable_thinking toggle / reasoning_effort, with NO numeric per-request cap. Quant: GGUF Q4_K_M (~20GB) and MLX 4-bit available. [uncertain on exact average thinking-token count per paper-critique task]
qwen3_verdict: Qwen/Qwen3-32B (May 2025 dense release) is a hybrid thinking model with thinking ENABLED by default. Its per-request control surface is more mature and uniform than Gemma 4's. Two mechanisms: (1) the enable_thinking flag, passed via chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false} per-request in vLLM (extra_body in OpenAI client) or set server-wide with --default-chat-template-kwargs; request-level always overrides server default; works correctly in vLLM >= 0.9.0 with --reasoning-parser qwen3 (older vLLM <=0.8.5 silently ignored it). (2) the soft switch: appending /think or /no_think to the system or user message toggles thinking per-turn, with the model following the most recent instruction in multi-turn chats. On a numeric per-request budget cap (the Gemma-4 thinking_budget_tokens equivalent), Qwen3's story is uneven: the Qwen3 technical report itself describes 'Thinking Control' with an explicit token budget, and llama.cpp's thinking_budget_tokens works for Qwen3 (it was actually discussed for Qwen3.5). NVIDIA NIM exposes nvext.max_thinking_tokens (a BudgetControlLogitsProcessor forces </think> at the cap, with a 10% extension window for sentence completion). BUT enforcement is framework-dependent and buggy in places: SGLang has a documented open bug where thinking_budget is accepted but NOT enforced (a 200-token budget still produced ~1400 reasoning tokens, leaving content:null), and HuggingFace transformers only recently added max_thinking_tokens (PR #42112). Measured thinking volume: ~910 mean thinking tokens / ~1,573 total output tokens on a temporal-reasoning task; non-thinking mode ~609 output tokens, 0 thinking. Thinking mode generates 2-3x more tokens (and ~2-3x slower tok/s) than no-think. Text-only. Quant: GGUF Q4_K_M and MLX 4-bit widely available.
benchmarks: Thinking-on vs thinking-off quality (the dimension that matters here). Gemma 4 31B (thinking mode): GPQA Diamond ~84.3% (model card), MMLU-Pro ~85.2%, AIME 2026 89.2%, LiveCodeBench v6 80.0%, BigBench Extra Hard 74.4% — these are huge jumps over Gemma 3 27B's thinking-off-era numbers (GPQA 42.4%, AIME 20.8%), confirming thinking mode is the primary driver of Gemma 4's expert-reasoning gains. Qwen3-32B (thinking mode, official Qwen3-VL report): GPQA Diamond 68.4, MMLU-Pro 79.1, AIME-25 72.9, LiveCodeBench v6 60.6; Qwen's own technical report shows Pass@1 on AIME24/AIME25/LiveCodeBench/GPQA Diamond rising monotonically with thinking budget for the 32B. Non-thinking mode for both is materially worse on math/science/logic but adequate and 2-5x cheaper on retrieval/extraction/classification/short-form Q&A. Per the overthinking literature, thinking mode gives little-to-no benefit (and can hurt via over-analysis) on writing, summarization, and tool-dispatch tasks. So: thinking ON for planning/critique/synthesis nodes; thinking OFF for tool-dispatch nodes — which is exactly Labmate's intended split. [uncertain — no head-to-head academic-writing-quality eval isolating thinking-on vs thinking-off for these two exact models]
factual_accuracy: Thinking mode reduces hallucination on hard-science reasoning for both models — the GPQA Diamond / AIME gains are themselves largely thinking-mode-driven (extended CoT, self-consistency, verification). For a paper-critique task, thinking-on lets either model check claims against the supplied text before committing, lowering confabulation versus a snap answer. Caveat from the efficiency literature: more sophisticated reasoning can also mask remaining hallucinations more convincingly (confident-but-wrong), and overthinking can cause a model to abandon a previously correct answer. Neither model publishes a SimpleQA/TruthfulQA delta isolating thinking-on vs thinking-off, so the factuality benefit is inferential rather than a measured per-model number. For Labmate, thinking-on for critique is still the safer default for factual rigor; pair with RAG over the actual paper rather than parametric recall for either model. [uncertain — no measured thinking-on vs thinking-off factuality delta for either model]
inference_speed: Thinking mode is the dominant latency/cost lever. Qwen3-32B-AWQ generates 2-3x more tokens per second in no-think than in think mode, and think mode produces 2-3x more total tokens — so thinking-off is roughly an order-of-magnitude cheaper end-to-end on simple requests. Gemma 4 31B thinking mode can emit 4,000+ reasoning tokens (community report: 20-73s per task on a 16GB M1 Mac). This is precisely why per-request control matters for Labmate: tool-dispatch nodes should run thinking-off (fast, ~600 output tokens for Qwen3) while planning/critique nodes run thinking-on. A numeric per-request budget (llama.cpp thinking_budget_tokens, NIM nvext.max_thinking_tokens) caps worst-case latency on a 'think but don't overthink' middle tier. Gemma 4 ships a speculative-decoding draft model that further speeds generation. Reasoning models are reported 10-74x more expensive to operate than non-reasoning counterparts on AIME-class tasks, underscoring the value of toggling off for non-reasoning work. [uncertain — no fixed-hardware tok/s figure for Gemma 4 31B thinking vs non-thinking specifically]
multimodal_support: Not the focus of this dimension, but relevant for routing: Gemma 4 31B is natively multimodal (text + image + figures/charts + OCR), so a paper-critique node can read embedded figures AND run thinking mode over them in one pass. Qwen3-32B is text-only (vision lives in the separate Qwen3-VL line), so figure-heavy critique would need a separate VL model regardless of thinking setting. Gemma 4 also has a SEPARATE visual token budget (supported values 70/140/280/560/1120 tokens per image) that is unrelated to the reasoning/thinking budget — do not confuse the two when configuring per-request control.
context_window: Thinking traces consume context: Qwen3's reasoning_content does not count toward the visible reply but DOES consume context tokens, and Qwen guidance is to strip prior-turn reasoning from history to preserve room. A long paper-critique thinking trace (~900-4,000+ tokens) eats meaningfully into the window. Gemma 4 31B's 256K native context absorbs this comfortably across a multi-paper session; Qwen3-32B's 32K native (extensible to 128K via YaRN) is tighter once full papers plus multi-thousand-token thinking traces are stacked. For Labmate, this favors keeping thinking-on critique nodes on Gemma 4's larger window, or aggressively pruning thinking traces from Qwen3 history. [uncertain — no measured effective-context-under-thinking figure for either model]
non_cuda_support: Per-request thinking control is available on non-CUDA backends. llama.cpp (the primary non-CUDA path via Metal/ROCm/Vulkan) is exactly where thinking_budget_tokens lives, so AMD/Apple users get the numeric per-request budget for BOTH models — provided the server is launched WITHOUT --reasoning-budget (leave default -1). Caveats specific to non-CUDA llama.cpp: Gemma 4 has reported <unused49> token-flood bugs at long context, and enable_thinking:false is silently ignored for Gemma 4 in llama-server (must use global --reasoning off). MLX (Apple Silicon) exposes enable_thinking via apply_chat_template for both. vLLM ROCm supports the enable_thinking / reasoning_effort toggles for Gemma 4 and the enable_thinking toggle for Qwen3. Both have GGUF Q4_K_M/Q5_K_M quants. Net: full thinking-control surface is reachable on non-CUDA, but Gemma 4's llama.cpp quirks make Qwen3 the lower-friction choice on AMD/Apple. [uncertain — Gemma 4 llama.cpp thinking-flag bugs may be fixed in newer builds than reviewed]
over_refusal_risk: Not directly a function of thinking mode, but worth noting: thinking traces occasionally surface the refusal-reasoning explicitly, which can make a thinking-on model MORE likely to talk itself into refusing a borderline dual-use research query, whereas thinking-off gives a faster direct answer. Both models carry real over-refusal risk on biosafety/dual-use/medical topics (Gemma 4 reported as 'strongly censored'; Qwen3 also has a 'very strong refusal rate'). For sensitive-but-legitimate critique tasks, this is a minor argument for testing thinking-off behavior as well. [uncertain — no study isolating refusal-rate-under-thinking vs no-thinking for either model]
ecosystem_toolchain: This is where the comparison is decided. Qwen3's per-request thinking control is the more reliable and flexible of the two: a clean enable_thinking flag (chat_template_kwargs, request overrides server default in vLLM >= 0.9.0), a /think /no_think soft switch usable per-turn from inside the prompt (no API plumbing needed), and a documented token-budget concept (thinking_budget / nvext.max_thinking_tokens on NIM, thinking_budget_tokens in llama.cpp). Gemma 4's control is fragmented across backends: vLLM uses enable_thinking / reasoning_effort but offers NO numeric per-request cap; llama.cpp uses thinking_budget_tokens (numeric cap) but ignores enable_thinking:false (requires global --reasoning off), so you cannot cleanly toggle per-request AND cap in the same llama.cpp config the way you can reason about Qwen3. Both have known enforcement bugs (SGLang ignores Qwen3 thinking_budget; llama.cpp leaks Gemma 4 thinking / floods unused tokens). vLLM parser flags: --reasoning-parser gemma4 for Gemma 4, --reasoning-parser qwen3 for Qwen3. On flexibility + reliability of the thinking toggle, Qwen3 wins; on raw thinking-on quality for science, Gemma 4 wins.
labmate_relevance: HIGH. Labmate's LangGraph design explicitly needs per-node reasoning control: planning/paper-critique/synthesis nodes require deep thinking, while tool-dispatch nodes require fast direct responses. A reliable, flexible per-request thinking toggle is therefore a first-class deployment requirement, not a nicety — it directly governs latency, cost, and output quality of the whole orchestrator loop. The numeric budget cap (thinking_budget_tokens) additionally lets Labmate bound worst-case latency on 'think a little' middle-tier nodes.
recommendation: Architect Labmate to toggle thinking PER NODE, not per model. For tool-dispatch nodes: thinking OFF (fast, ~600 output tokens, no benefit from CoT on dispatch per the overthinking literature). For planning / paper-critique / research-synthesis nodes: thinking ON. Implementation by chosen brain: (A) If Gemma 4 31B on llama.cpp (Labmate's stated stack): launch the server WITHOUT --reasoning-budget (leave -1) so per-request thinking_budget_tokens is honored; use a generous thinking_budget_tokens (e.g. 2,000-4,000) on critique nodes and a small one (or global --reasoning off on a second server) for dispatch nodes — do NOT rely on enable_thinking:false via chat_template_kwargs for Gemma 4 in llama-server, it is silently ignored. If on vLLM instead, use reasoning_effort (high for critique, none for dispatch) since vLLM lacks a numeric Gemma 4 cap. (B) Qwen3-32B offers the more reliable/flexible toggle: enable_thinking per request (vLLM >= 0.9.0) plus /think//no_think soft switches, and thinking_budget_tokens (llama.cpp) / nvext.max_thinking_tokens (NIM) for numeric caps — but verify enforcement on your serving framework (AVOID SGLang's thinking_budget, it is not enforced). Model-switching strategy: keep Gemma 4 31B (thinking-on) for figure-heavy paper critique and the hardest science reasoning where its GPQA ~84% beats Qwen3-32B's 68.4; use Qwen3-32B where you want the cleaner, framework-portable thinking toggle and tighter budget enforcement for cost-controlled middle-tier nodes. Whichever is chosen, leave the server-wide --reasoning-budget UNSET so per-request budgets work, and strip prior thinking traces from conversation history to conserve context. If forced to pick one model purely on thinking-control reliability/flexibility (this dimension), Qwen3 is the lower-risk choice; if picking on thinking-on output quality for science, Gemma 4 wins.
